title: Science Snapshots: July 26, 2026
summary: Three short science items: astronomers report a very large moon-like object orbiting a brown dwarf around star CD-35 2722, a study finds invasive species cause greater environmental damage per species in the Global South, and researchers used AlphaFold3 to build ContactSeek, an AI-guided tool that improves DNA base editing accuracy.

An artist’s illustration of the system around the brown dwarf CD-35 2722 B, with the newfound moon-like object at the centre. The star left has about half the mass of our sun, and it is orbited by a brown dwarf right. Photo Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser

First exomoon found comes with a challenge

Using the radial velocity method, astronomers have identified a large body orbiting the brown dwarf CD-35 2722 B, which itself orbits a star. The object is estimated to be about 90 percent as massive as Jupiter and completes an orbit around the brown dwarf every 170 days on an elliptical path. The discovery marks a milestone in the search for moons beyond the solar system and raises difficult questions for current classification schemes, because the object is so massive that it blurs the line between a moon and a planet.

Invasive species affect the Global South more

A new study finds that the environmental consequences of invasive species are more severe per species in the Global South than in wealthier nations. Previous thinking held that the Global North faced the greater threat because it reported more invasive species, but researchers say that pattern largely reflects wealthier countries conducting more studies. The authors report that damage per invasive species is substantially higher in the Global South, driven by factors such as rapid trade growth and weaker environmental oversight and response capacity.

AI helps take next stride on proteins in medicine

Researchers have developed a tool called ContactSeek to enhance DNA base editing. Base editing is a gene therapy technique that can precisely change individual DNA bases, but it often produces off-target edits when parts of the editor protein interact unpredictably with DNA. The team used the AI protein folding model AlphaFold3 to predict the likelihood that specific residues of editor proteins will contact DNA, finding predictions from the model to be more sensitive than existing 3D models. Using these insights they designed improved variants of common editors, including versions of Cas9, that reduce unintended edits.
